Stratify patients on the basis of their risk to develop major thrombotic complications. C

background.definition: Polycythemia vera (PV) is a Philadelphia chromosome (Ph)-negative chronic myeloproliferative disorders (MPD) characterized by clonal tri-lineage bone marrow hypercellularity and increased red-cell mass. See for diagnostic criteria. Essential thrombocythemia is a similar disorder characterized by thrombocythemia, but with normal hemoglobin/hematocrit and no evidence of myelofibrosis, CML, or iron deficiency.

list.listitem: About 1 to 3 per 100,000 persons per year (data from a Swedish population).
Approximately 30 per 100,000 person-years (95% CI, 6-87).
Mutation in the Janus kinase 2 gene is present in almost all patients with PV.
Hematopoietic progenitors derived from patients with PV are hypersensitive to the stimulation of physiological growth factors, such as erythropoietin, leading to excessive bone marrow proliferation.

This hypersensitivity is mainly due to an acquired point mutation (V617F) in the Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) gene present in more than 95% of patients with PV. JAK2, a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase, is critical for driving intracellular signaling by the growth factors receptors. The mutation leads to constitutive, growth factor independent, activation of JAK2. The result is increased sensitivity of megakaryocytes to erythropoietin (EPO), increasing production of red blood cells, platelets, and white blood cells, and a feedback loop that leads to lower levels of EPO in response.
Other mutations, located in the exon 12 of JAK2, have been reported in rare V617F-negative PV patients.
Essential thrombocythemia is associated with the same genetic defect; about half of patients have the JAK2 mutation.
Diagnose polycythemia vera according to the updated 2007 WHO criteria (). C
Obtain molecular testing for the JAK2 V617F mutation in all patients with increased hemoglobin/hematocrit values and no obvious evidence of secondary polycythemia. C
Use bone marrow biopsy and serum erythropoietin level to confirm the diagnosis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Absence of JAK2 V617F mutation or other functionally similar mutations
Presence of Philadelphia chromosome and/or BCR/ABL
Characteristic bone marrow histology and frequent cytogenetic abnormalities

list.listitem: See for the revised World Health Organization diagnostic criteria.
The median age at diagnosis is 59 years.

Suspect polycythemia vera (PV) in patients with erythrocytosis and thrombocytosis. Order diagnostic tests (below) for patients with increased hemoglobin/hematocrit values without evident causes of secondary polycythemia, such as respiratory insufficiency.
Splenomegaly and pruritus may be seen in patients with PV, and support the diagnosis.
Suspect the disorder in patients with hemoglobin greater than 18.5 g/dL in men and 16.5 g/dL in women.
Molecular testing of JAK2 V617F is the key assay to exclude secondary polycythemia. The presence of the mutation does not distinguish between PV and other myeloproliferative disorders.

Serum erythropoietin (EPO) is useful to confirm (low values) or exclude (high values) the diagnosis. A value <3.3 IU/L was 87% sensitive and 97% specific in one series of 241 patients, using a reference standard of bone marrow biopsy.
See for a suggested approach that integrates testing for the V617F mutation, EPO, and selective use of bone marrow biopsy.

Bone marrow biopsy enhances diagnostic reliability, but morphological examination should be performed by an experienced pathologist. Assay for endogenous erythropoietin colonies is specific but time-consuming and requires a specialized laboratory.
Red blood cell mass, previously considered a major diagnostic tool, is becoming less important in the era of molecular assays because of suboptimal accuracy and demanding work-up.
See algorithm in for a suggested approach to diagnosis.

In patients who are negative for the V617F mutation and with normal or elevated EPO levels, consider secondary thrombocythemia: (1) Hypoxia-driven: chronic lung disease, cardiopulmonary shunt, tobacco, high altitude, or sleep apnea; (2) Oxygen independent: cancer or drugs such as androgens or EPO; or (3) Congenital: high 02 affinity Hb, "Chuvash" polycythemia, or EPO receptor mutation.
Patients should be stratified according to the risk of developing major thrombotic complications. C
Low-risk patients (age <60 years and no history of thrombosis) should be treated with phlebotomy and low-dose aspirin. A

High-risk patients (age 60+ years and/or history of thrombotic event) should be given myelosuppressive drugs: hydroxyurea as first choice, B and interferon-alpha in selected patients. Ruxolitinib is a good alternative in patients who do not tolerate standard therapy or in whom it is unsuccessful.B

Patients with PV should be stratified according to the risk to develop thrombotic complications. At least one of the following defines the high-risk category: age above 60 years or a previous thrombotic event.

Low-risk patients (age under 60 years and no history of thrombosis) should be treated with phlebotomy, aimed at maintaining hematocrit values below 45%, and aspirin 100 mg daily.A Cochrane systematic review found a non-significant reduction in fatal thrombotic events (OR 0.2, 95% CI, 0.03-1.14) and no increase in the risk of major bleeding with aspirin.

A systematic review identified 10 observational studies of anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents, with or without cytoreduction, in patients with PV, essential thrombocytopenia, and myelofibrosis. The greatest reduction was seen with direct-acting oral anticoagulants plus cytoreduction. However, studies were at high risk of bias and there have been no RCTs. However, the apparently greater benefit with a DOAC must be balanced against a greater risk of bleeding.

High-risk patients include those who are 60 years or older, have a history of thrombosis, or who develop progressive myeloproliferation as indicated by rapidly increasing splenomegaly and/or leukocytosis and/or thrombocytosis. They should be treated with cytoreductive therapy in addition to low-dose aspirin. Hydroxyurea (HU) is the first-line therapy, with a starting dose of 15 mg/kg/day followed by a maintenance dose to keep hematocrit <45% without reducing leukocytes below 3000 cells/mm3. Interferon-alpha is indicated in high-risk patients <40 years or intolerant to HU. This drug is given at the starting dose of 3 million units daily followed by a maintanance dose adjusted to the lowest weekly level to maintain hematocrit <45%.
A systematic review concluded that pegylated and non-pegylated interferon were similarly effective. The overall response rate was 81% (95% CI 77% to 84%) with complete hematologic response in 49%.

An RCT in over 800 patients with essential thrombocythemia randomized them to aspirin plus either hydroxyurea or anegrelide. After median 39 months, rates of arterial thrombosis, myelofibrosis, and serious hemorrhage were higher with anegrelide. Thus, hydroxyurea is the preferred agent for these patients.
Specific JAK2 V617F inhibitors have been developed and are currently being evaluated in phase I/II clinical studies.

One of these is ruxolitinib (Jakafi), which was evaluated in 222 patients who were phlebotomy dependent due to an inadequate response to hydroxyurea or intolerance of the drug (intolerance occurs in approximately 20% of patients). The primary endpoint was hematologic and reduction in spleen volume, and was achieved more often in the ruxolitinib group (21% vs 1%, NNT = 5). Thromboembolic events were less common in treated patients, but the study was underpowered for this outcome (1 vs 6 events).

Rusferrtide is an injected drug that reduces the availability of iron for erythropoiesis. In the first part of the study, 70 patients were given rusfertide in a dose-finding evaluation. In part 2, they were randomized to rusfertide or placebo. Patients given rusfertide had a large reduction in phlebotomies per year, from 8.7 to 0.6 per year. Symptoms also improved more and adverse events were generally mild.

Consider splenectomy for patients with portal hypertension that is symptomatic, those who require frequent transfusions, and patients with painful splenomegaly that is not successfully treated medically.
Rarely, apheresis has been used to reduce platelet counts in patients with essential thrombocythemia who have extremely high platelet levels and are pregnant or require surgery.

Arterial and venous thrombosis: manage according to standard practice. Life-long warfarin (PT INR therapeutic range 2.0-3.0) is recommended in patients with abdominal vein thrombosis. Risk of thrombosis is increased with recently diagnosed polycythemia vera, age over 60 years, history of thrombosis, and higher levels of hematocrit. A systematic review identified 10 observational studies of anticoagulants and antiplatelet agents, with or without cytoreduction, in patients with PV, essential thrombocytopenia, and myelofibrosis. The greatest reduction was seen with direct-acting oral anticoagulants plus cytoreduction. However, studies were at high risk of bias and there have been no RCTs.
Severe microvascular circulation symptoms ( i.e., erythromelalgia): treat with a loading dose of aspirin (300-500 mg per day) followed by a maintenance dose (100 mg per day).

Pruritus: options include antihistamines (cyproheptadine 4-16 mg per day), interferon-alpha (3 million units s.c. 3 times a week), paroxetine (20 mg per day) and photochemotherapy using psoralen and ultraviolet A light.
Spinal cord infarction with heavy physical exertion has been reported.
Pulmonary hypertension is a common comorbidity in patients with PV and essential thrombocytopenia. The prevalence estimates in a systematic review ranged from 4% to 58%.

Major disease-related causes of death are cardiovascular complications (45%) and hematological transformations into post-polycythemia myelofibrosis or acute leukemia (13%). In the past, untreated patients showed an high incidence of thrombotic events and a life expectancy of about 18 months after diagnosis. Overall mortality is about 20% higher than expected in age and sex-matched general population, with worse outcomes in elderly, those with thrombosis, and those with leukocytosis. B
In 7 cohorts the median survival from diagnosis was 14 to 28 years.B

The presence of luekocytosis increases the likelihood of leukemic or fibrotic transformation (i.e., development of AML, myelodysplastic syndrome, or myelofibrosis). It also increased the risk of thrombosis, especially over 9.4 cells/109/L.B
A follow-up visit including history, physical examination, and complete blood cell counts is recommended at least every 3-6 months. C
At least one of the following defines high-risk pregnancy: previous thrombosis or previous severe pregnancy complications, including poliabortivity, preeclampsia, intrauterine death, or stillbirth.
Low risk pregnancy is managed with phlebotomy to maintain hematocrit <45%, aspirin 100 mg per day and low-molecular-weight heparin 4000 U/day for 6 weeks after delivery.
High-risk pregnancy is managed as above plus low-molecular-weight heparin 4000 U/day throughout pregnancy.
In case of progressive myeloproliferation, as above defined, the drug of choice is interferon-alpha.

PV is rare in children. A case series identified 35 patients in the medical literature. Of this group, 7 had Budd-Chiari syndrome, one stroke, one gangrene, and three severe hemorrage. Leukocytosis was present in about a quarter of patients.

feature.caption: Proposed Revised WHO Criteria for Polycythemia Vera. Diagnosis requires the presence or both major criteria and 1 minor criterion or the presence of the first major criterion together with 2 minor criteria.

tr.th: 1. Hemoglobin >18.5 g/dL in men, 16.5 in women or other evidence of increased red cell volume

td.strong: 2. Presence of JAK2617V>F or other functionally similar mutation such as JAK2 exon 12 mutation

tr.td: 1. Bone marrow biopsy showing hypercellularity for age with trilineage growth (panmyelosis) with prominent erythroid, granulocytic, and megakaryocytic proliferation
2. Serum erythropoietin level below the reference range for normal
3. Endogenous erythroid colony formation in vivo
